1: # Application Folder
2: 
3: ## Contents
4: 
5: - General
6: - Directory Location
7: - Built-In Applications
8: - NuttShell (NSH) Built-In Commands
9: - Synchronous Built-In Commands
10: - Application Configuration File
11: - Example Built-In Application
12: - Building NuttX with Board-Specific Pieces Outside the Source Tree
13: 
14: ## General
15: 
16: This folder provides various applications found in sub-directories. These
17: applications are not inherently a part of NuttX but are provided to help you
18: develop your own applications. The `apps/` directory is a _break away_ part of
19: the configuration that you may choose to use or not.
20: 
21: ## Directory Location
22: 
23: The default application directory used by the NuttX build should be named
24: `apps/` (or `apps-x.y.z/` where `x.y.z` is the NuttX version number). This
25: `apps/` directory should appear in the directory tree at the same level as the
26: NuttX directory. Like:
27: 
28: ```
29:  .
30:  |- nuttx
31:  |
32:  `- apps
33: ```
34: 
35: If all of the above conditions are TRUE, then NuttX will be able to find the
36: application directory. If your application directory has a different name or is
37: location at a different position, then you will have to inform the NuttX build
38: system of that location. There are several ways to do that:
39: 
40: 1) You can define `CONFIG_APPS_DIR` to be the full path to your application
41:    directory in the NuttX configuration file.
42: 2) You can provide the path to the application directory on the command line
43:    like: `make APPDIR=<path>` or `make CONFIG_APPS_DIR=<path>`
44: 3) When you configure NuttX using `tools/configure.sh`, you can provide that
45:    path to the application directory on the configuration command line like:
46:    `./configure.sh -a <app-dir> <board-name>:<config-name>`
47: 
48: ## Built-In Applications
49: 
50: NuttX also supports applications that can be started using a name string. In
51: this case, application entry points with their requirements are gathered
52: together in two files:
53: 
54: - `builtin/builtin_proto.h` – Entry points, prototype function
55: - `builtin/builtin_list.h` – Application specific information and requirements
56: 
57: The build occurs in several phases as different build targets are executed: (1)
58: context, (2) depend, and (3) default (all). Application information is collected
59: during the make context build phase.
60: 
61: To execute an application function:
62: 
63: `exec_builtin()` is defined in the `apps/include/builtin/builtin.h`.
64: 
65: ## NuttShell (NSH) Built-In Commands
66: 
67: One use of builtin applications is to provide a way of invoking your custom
68: application through the NuttShell (NSH) command line. NSH will support a
69: seamless method invoking the applications, when the following option is enabled
70: in the NuttX configuration file:
71: 
72: ```conf
73: CONFIG_NSH_BUILTIN_APPS=y
74: ```
75: 
76: Applications registered in the `apps/builtin/builtin_list.h` file will then be
77: accessible from the NSH command line. If you type `help` at the NSH prompt, you
78: will see a list of the registered commands.
79: 
80: ## Synchronous Built-In Commands
81: 
82: By default, built-in commands started from the NSH command line will run
83: asynchronously with NSH. If you want to force NSH to execute commands then wait
84: for the command to execute, you can enable that feature by adding the following
85: to the NuttX configuration file:
86: 
87: ```conf
88: CONFIG_SCHED_WAITPID=y
89: ```
90: 
91: The configuration option enables support for the `waitpid()` RTOS interface.
92: When that interface is enabled, NSH will use it to wait, sleeping until the
93: built-in command executes to completion.
94: 
95: Of course, even with `CONFIG_SCHED_WAITPID=y` defined, specific commands can
96: still be forced to run asynchronously by adding the ampersand (`&`) after the
97: NSH command.
98: 
99: ## Application Configuration File
100: 
101: The NuttX configuration uses `kconfig-frontends` tools and the NuttX
102: configuration file (`.config`) file. For example, the NuttX `.config` may have:
103: 
104: ```conf
105: CONFIG_EXAMPLES_HELLO=y
106: ```
107: 
108: This will select the `apps/examples/hello` in the following way:
109: 
110: - The top-level make will include `apps/examples/Make.defs`
111: - `apps/examples/Make.defs` will set `CONFIGURED_APPS += $(APPDIR)/examples/hello`
112:   like this:
113: 
114: ```makefile
115:   ifneq ($(CONFIG_EXAMPLES_HELLO),)
116:   CONFIGURED_APPS += $(APPDIR)/examples/hello
117:   endif
118: ```
119: 
120: ## Example Built-In Application
121: 
122: An example application skeleton can be found under the `examples/hello`
123: sub-directory. This example shows how a builtin application can be added to the
124: project. One must:
125: 
126:  1. Create sub-directory as: progname
127: 
128:  2. In this directory there should be:
129: 
130:     - A `Make.defs` file that would be included by the `apps/Makefile`
131:     - A `Kconfig` file that would be used by the configuration tool (see the
132:       file `kconfig-language.txt` in the NuttX tools repository). This `Kconfig`
133:       file should be included by the `apps/Kconfig` file
134:     - A `Makefile`, and
135:     - The application source code.
136: 
137:  3. The application source code should provide the entry point:
138: 
139:     ```c
140:     main()
141:     ```
142: 
143:  4. Set the requirements in the file: `Makefile`, specially the lines:
144: 
145:     ```makefile
146:     PROGNAME   = progname
147:     PRIORITY   = SCHED_PRIORITY_DEFAULT
148:     STACKSIZE  = 768
149:     ASRCS      = asm source file list as a.asm b.asm ...
150:     CSRCS      = C source file list as foo1.c foo2.c ..
151:     ```
152: 
153:  5. The `Make.defs` file should include a line like:
154: 
155:     ```makefile
156:     ifneq ($(CONFIG_PROGNAME),)
157:     CONFIGURED_APPS += progname
158:     endif
159:     ```
160: 
161: ## Building NuttX with Board-Specific Pieces Outside the Source Tree
162: 
163: Q: Has anyone come up with a tidy way to build NuttX with board- specific pieces
164:    outside the source tree?
165: 
166: A: Here are three:
167: 
168:    1) There is a make target called `make export`. It will build NuttX, then
169:       bundle all of the header files, libraries, startup objects, and other
170:       build components into a `.zip` file. You can move that `.zip` file into
171:       any build environment you want. You can even build NuttX under a DOS `CMD`
172:       window.
173: 
174:       This make target is documented in the top level `nuttx/README.txt`.
175: 
176:    2) You can replace the entire `apps/` directory. If there is nothing in the
177:       `apps/` directory that you need, you can define `CONFIG_APPS_DIR` in your
178:       `.config` file so that it points to a different, custom application
179:       directory.
180: 
181:       You can copy any pieces that you like from the old apps/directory to your
182:       custom apps directory as necessary.
183: 
184:       This is documented in `NuttX/boards/README.txt` and `NuttX Porting Guide`
185:       online at <https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/NUTTX/Porting+Guide>.
186: 
187:    3) If you like the random collection of stuff in the `apps/` directory but
188:       just want to expand the existing components with your own, external
189:       sub-directory then there is an easy way to that too: You just create a
190:       symbolic link in the `apps/` directory that redirects to your application
191:       sub-directory.
192: 
193:       In order to be incorporated into the build, the directory that you link
194:       under the `apps/` directory should contain (1) a `Makefile` that supports
195:       the `clean` and `distclean` targets (see other `Makefile`s for examples),
196:       and (2) a tiny `Make.defs` file that simply adds the custom build
197:       directories to the variable `CONFIGURED_APPS` like:
198: 
199:       ```makefile
200:       CONFIGURED_APPS += my_directory1 my_directory2
201:       ```
202: 
203:       The `apps/Makefile` will always automatically check for the existence of
204:       subdirectories containing a `Makefile` and a `Make.defs` file. The
205:       `Makefile` will be used only to support cleaning operations. The Make.defs
206:       file provides the set of directories to be built; these directories must
207:       also contain a `Makefile`. That `Makefile` must be able to build the
208:       sources and add the objects to the `apps/libapps.a` archive. (see other
209:       `Makefile`s for examples). It should support the all, install, context,
210:       and depend targets.
211: 
212:       `apps/Makefile` does not depend on any hardcoded lists of directories.
213:       Instead, it does a wildcard search to find all appropriate directories.
214:       This means that to install a new application, you simply have to copy the
215:       directory (or link it) into the `apps/` directory. If the new directory
216:       includes a `Makefile` and `Make.defs` file, then it will automatically be
217:       included in the build.
218: 
219:       If the directory that you add also includes a `Kconfig` file, then it will
220:       automatically be included in the NuttX configuration system as well.
221:       `apps/Makefile` uses a tool at `apps/tools/mkkconfig.sh` that dynamically
222:       builds the `apps/Kconfig` file at pre-configuration time.
223: 
224:       You could, for example, create a script called `install.sh` that installs
225:       a custom application, configuration, and board specific directory:
226: 
227:       a) Copy `MyBoard` directory to `boards/MyBoard`.
228:       b) Add a symbolic link to `MyApplication` at `apps/external`.
229:       c) Configure NuttX, usually by:
230: 
231:       ```bash
232:       tools/configure.sh MyBoard:MyConfiguration
233:       ```
234: 
235:       Use of the name `apps/external` is suggested because that name is included
236:       in the `.gitignore` file and will save you some nuisance when working with
237:       GIT.
238:

Driver Internal Structure 6: 7: The driver framework of openvela is relatively simple and does not provide a complex driver model like that in the Linux system (such as Device, Driver, Bus, Class, etc.). Compared with Linux, the driver framework of openvela has the following characteristics: 8: 9: - Driver registration interface: Register the driver with the VFS (Virtual File System) through a simple driver registration interface. 10: - Implementation of function set: Implement the `file_operations` operation function set for upper-layer calls. 11: - System call support: Upper-layer applications indirectly call underlying drivers to complete device operations through standard system calls. 12: 13: This simplified design makes the driver framework of openvela easier to understand and implement. 14: 15: ### 1. Driver Types and Hierarchical Structure 16: 17: openvela supports multiple device drivers, which are mainly divided into the following types: 18: 19: - Character device drivers: zero, null, sensor, adc, etc. 20: - Block device drivers: emmc, sd card, bch, etc. 21: - Special device drivers: mtd, ptp, timer, netdev, etc. 22: 23: The following is the workflow diagram of openvela drivers, showing the complete path from the application program to the hardware: 24: 25: 26: 27: Among them, drivers are divided into two layers according to functions: 28: 29: 1. Upper Half (provided by openvela) 30: 31: - The driver registers itself with the openvela system through `register_driver` or `register_blockdriver`. 32: - Provide high-level system call interfaces (such as `read`, `write`, `close`, etc.). 33: - Interact with the Lower Half through the operation set functions. 34: 35: 2. Lower Half (implemented by driver developers) 36: 37: - Responsible for implementing interactions with hardware devices and architectures. 38: - Involves specific operations of underlying hardware such as buses and peripherals. 39: - Defines the core operation logic of the device driver, and driver developers need to implement the corresponding interfaces according to specific devices. 40: 41: ### 2. Characteristics of the Driver Model 42: 43: Compared with the Linux device driver model, the driver model of openvela is more simplified and has the following characteristics: 44: 45: - No matching and probing mechanisms: There is no matching and probing process of `bus`, `device`, and `driver` in openvela. 46: - No device types and device numbers: The concepts of device types or device numbers (major/minor) are not used. 47: - No module_init initialization function: The driver initialization function needs to be explicitly called in the board code for initialization. 48: - Device node registration: In openvela, there are no interfaces like `cdev_add` or `device_create`, and the driver is registered through the `register_driver()` or `register_blockdriver()` interface. 49: 50: This design significantly reduces the complexity of the driver model, making openvela more suitable for resource-constrained MCU (Microcontroller Unit) environments. 51: 52: ### 3. Pseudo Root File System 53: 54: The device drivers of openvela rely on the Pseudo Root File System, similar to `/dev` (`devtmpfs`) in Linux. However, it differs from Linux in the following aspects: 55: 56: - RAM-only usage: Does not depend on storage media or block device drivers. 57: - Device nodes are not actual files: Device nodes are just entries of devices in the root file system, indicating that the devices have been initialized and are available for use. 58: 59: In other words, only device drivers can create device nodes, and the existence of device nodes indicates that the devices have been registered and are ready. 60: 61: 62: 63: ### 4. Driver Directory Structure 64: 65: According to the types of drivers, openvela places driver code in different directories: 66: 67: - Shareable drivers: Stored in the `drivers` directory, suitable for general device drivers. 68: - Custom drivers: Stored in the board-level directory `nuttx/boards////src`. 69: 70: ### 5. Non-standard Interface: `boardctl` 71: 72: In addition to character device drivers, openvela provides a non-standard OS interface `boardctl` for application programs to control board-level logic through the `ioctl` method. Common functions include: 73: 74: - Board-level initialization: `board_app_init`, `board_app_finalinit` 75: - Power management: `board_poweroff`, `board_pmctl` 76: - System reset: `board_reset` 77: 78: **Note**: Under normal circumstances, application programs should control board-level logic through the `ioctl` interface of character device drivers instead of directly calling `boardctl`. 79: 80: ## II. Data Structures and Interfaces 81: 82: ### 1. Data Structures 83: 84: In openvela, the application layer accesses drivers through system calls, with the calling process as follows: 85: 86: **System call -> VFS (Virtual File System) -> Driver**. 87: 88: To understand how drivers are registered with the file system, it is necessary to first understand the relevant data structures. The definitions of these data structures are located in the [include/nuttx/fs/fs.h](../../../../../../nuttx/blob/trunk-5.5/include/nuttx/fs/fs.h) file. 89: 90: #### Driver Registration and `inode` 91: 92: When a driver is registered with the file system, an `inode` is created and associated with the device file. The inode is the core data structure in the file system used to represent files or devices. The following describes the key fields and operation function sets related to driver registration. 93: 94: ```c 95: struct inode 96: { 97: FAR struct inode *i_parent; /* Link to parent level inode */ 98: FAR struct inode *i_peer; /* Link to same level inode */ 99: FAR struct inode *i_child; /* Link to lower level inode */ 100: atomic_short i_crefs; /* References to inode */ 101: uint16_t i_flags; /* Flags for inode */ 102: union inode_ops_u u; /* Inode operations */ 103: ino_t i_ino; /* Inode serial number */ 104: #if defined(CONFIG_PSEUDOFS_FILE) || defined(CONFIG_FS_SHMFS) 105: size_t i_size; /* The size of per inode driver */ 106: #endif 107: #ifdef CONFIG_PSEUDOFS_ATTRIBUTES 108: mode_t i_mode; /* Access mode flags */ 109: uid_t i_owner; /* Owner */ 110: gid_t i_group; /* Group */ 111: struct timespec i_atime; /* Time of last access */ 112: struct timespec i_mtime; /* Time of last modification */ 113: struct timespec i_ctime; /* Time of last status change */ 114: #endif 115: FAR void *i_private; /* Per inode driver private data */ 116: char i_name[1]; /* Name of inode (variable) */ 117: }; 118: ``` 119: 120: #### `i_flags` Field 121: 122: The `i_flags` field in the `struct inode` structure marks the file type of the `inode`, such as a driver file or message queue. To set or determine whether `i_flags` represents a driver file, the following macro definitions are provided: 123: 124: ```c 125: #define INODE_IS_DRIVER(i) INODE_IS_TYPE(i,FSNODEFLAG_TYPE_DRIVER) 126: 127: #define INODE_SET_DRIVER(i) INODE_SET_TYPE(i,FSNODEFLAG_TYPE_DRIVER) 128: ``` 129: 130: - `INODE_IS_DRIVER`: Determines whether the specified `inode` is a driver file. 131: - `INODE_SET_DRIVER`: Marks the specified `inode` as a driver file. 132: 133: #### `inode_ops_u` Field 134: 135: The `inode_ops_u` field in the `struct inode` structure is a union used to describe operation function sets. Depending on the type of `inode`, this field can contain one of the following operation function sets: 136: 137: - Character device driver operation function set. 138: - Block device driver operation function set. 139: - Mount point operation function set. 140: 141: ```cpp 142: union inode_ops_u 143: { 144: FAR const struct file_operations *i_ops; /* Driver operations for inode */ 145: #ifndef CONFIG_DISABLE_MOUNTPOINT 146: FAR const struct block_operations *i_bops; /* Block driver operations */ 147: FAR struct mtd_dev_s *i_mtd; /* MTD device driver */ 148: FAR const struct mountpt_operations *i_mops; /* Operations on a mountpoint */ 149: #endif 150: #ifdef CONFIG_FS_NAMED_SEMAPHORES 151: FAR struct nsem_inode_s *i_nsem; /* Named semaphore */ 152: #endif 153: #ifdef CONFIG_FS_NAMED_EVENTS 154: FAR struct nevent_inode_s *i_nevent; /* Named event */ 155: #endif 156: #ifdef CONFIG_PSEUDOFS_SOFTLINKS 157: FAR char *i_link; /* Full path to link target */ 158: #endif 159: }; 160: ``` 161: 162: #### Driver Operation Function Set 163: 164: The operation function set for character device drivers is defined by `struct file_operations`, with the following structure: 165: 166: ```c 167: struct file_operations 168: { 169: /* The device driver open method differs from the mountpoint open method */ 170: 171: CODE int (*open)(FAR struct file *filep); 172: 173: /* The following methods must be identical in signature and position 174: * because the struct file_operations and struct mountpt_operations are 175: * treated like unions. 176: */ 177: 178: CODE int (*close)(FAR struct file *filep); 179: CODE ssize_t (*read)(FAR struct file *filep, FAR char *buffer, 180: size_t buflen); 181: CODE ssize_t (*write)(FAR struct file *filep, FAR const char *buffer, 182: size_t buflen); 183: CODE off_t (*seek)(FAR struct file *filep, off_t offset, int whence); 184: CODE int (*ioctl)(FAR struct file *filep, int cmd, unsigned long arg); 185: CODE int (*mmap)(FAR struct file *filep, 186: FAR struct mm_map_entry_s *map); 187: CODE int (*truncate)(FAR struct file *filep, off_t length); 188: 189: CODE int (*poll)(FAR struct file *filep, FAR struct pollfd *fds, 190: bool setup); 191: CODE ssize_t (*readv)(FAR struct file *filep, FAR const struct uio *uio); 192: CODE ssize_t (*writev)(FAR struct file *filep, FAR const struct uio *uio); The following is the code implementation of the `register_driver` interface: 211: 212: ```c 213: /**************************************************************************** 214: * Name: register_driver 215: * 216: * Description: 217: * Register a character driver inode the pseudo file system. 218: * 219: * Input parameters: 220: * path - The path to the inode to create 221: * fops - The file operations structure 222: * mode - inmode priviledges (not used) 223: * priv - Private, user data that will be associated with the inode. 224: * 225: * Returned Value: 226: * Zero on success (with the inode point in 'inode'); A negated errno 227: * value is returned on a failure (all error values returned by 228: * inode_reserve): 229: * 230: * EINVAL - 'path' is invalid for this operation 231: * EEXIST - An inode already exists at 'path' 232: * ENOMEM - Failed to allocate in-memory resources for the operation 233: * 234: ****************************************************************************/ 235: 236: int register_driver(FAR const char *path, FAR const struct file_operations *fops, 237: mode_t mode, FAR void *priv) 238: { 239: FAR struct inode *node; 240: int ret; 241: 242: /* Insert a dummy node -- we need to hold the inode semaphore because we 243: * will have a momentarily bad structure. 244: */ 245: 246: inode_semtake(); 247: ret = inode_reserve(path, &node); 248: if (ret >= 0) 249: { 250: /* We have it, now populate it with driver specific information. 251: * NOTE that the initial reference count on the new inode is zero. 252: */ 253: 254: INODE_SET_DRIVER(node); 255: 256: node->u.i_ops = fops; 257: #ifdef CONFIG_FILE_MODE 258: node->i_mode = mode; 259: #endif 260: node->i_private = priv; 261: ret = OK; 262: } 263: 264: inode_semgive(); 265: return ret; 266: } 267: ``` 268: 269: #### Functional Description 270: 271: The main function of the `register_driver` interface is to register character device drivers with the pseudo file system. It performs the following key operations: 272: 273: 1. Create or find an inode. 274: 275: - According to the passed `path` parameter (usually corresponding to the device file path, such as `/dev/xxxx`), check if a corresponding inode exists. 276: - If not, create a new inode for the path. 277: 278: 2. Update the inode's driver information. 279: 280: - Update the actual driver-implemented `struct file_operations` (i.e., `fops`) into the inode. 281: - If permission configuration (`CONFIG_FILE_MODE`) is enabled, set the inode's permission information. 282: 283: 3. Set private data. 284: 285: - Store `priv` data in the inode's private field. 286: - This field is typically used to store the driver's private data, such as hardware-related context information. 287: 288: ## III. Example: ADC Driver Process Analysis 289: 290: In the driver code of openvela, drivers are typically divided into two parts: Upper half and Lower half. The following takes the ADC driver as an example to analyze its implementation process. 291: 292: ### 1. Driver Hierarchical Design 293: 294: 1. Upper Half 295: 296: - Provide general interfaces for application programs, mainly implementing the function set in `file_operations`. 297: - For the ADC driver, the `drivers/analog/adc.c` file describes the operation logic of the Upper Half. 298: - The implementation of the Upper Half is generic, suitable for all ADC devices, and does not require modification for specific hardware. 299: 300: 2. Lower Half 301: 302: - Hardware driver programs based on specific platforms, responsible for implementing hardware-level control, such as register operations. 303: - Implementations for specific hardware, such as the `arch/arm/src/lpc43xx/lpc43_adc.c` file, describe the ADC hardware driver for the LPC43xx platform. 304: 305: ### 2. Driver Framework 306: 307: The overall driver framework is shown in the following figure: 308: 309: 310: 311: 1. Chip-related (Lower Half): Red part (driver developer) 312: 313: - Responsible for actual hardware operations, such as register reading/writing and interrupt handling. 314: - In the interrupt handling function, it will callback the Upper Half interface, such as notifying the upper-layer application that data is ready through a message queue. 315: 316: 2. Generic Framework (Upper Half): Green part (provided by Vela) 317: 318: - Provide system call interfaces, such as `open`, `read`, etc. 319: - When implementing the `file_operations` function set, it will call the Lower Half interface to complete specific operations. 320: 321: 3. Board-level part: Orange part (driver developer) 322: 323: - Responsible for binding the Upper Half and Lower Half together, establishing connections, and registering them with the file system. 324: - Interfaces in this part are typically called during the system boot phase. 325: 326: ### 3. Implementation of Other Drivers 327: 328: The implementation mechanisms of other drivers in openvela are similar to the ADC driver, all adopting hierarchical design: 329: 330: - Upper Half: Docks with application system calls and provides general interfaces. 331: - Lower Half: Implements hardware-level operations and adapts to specific platforms. 332: 333: This hierarchical design is a reasonable approach with the following advantages: 334: 335: - Universality: The Upper Half, as a generic framework, does not need to be modified and is suitable for all similar devices. 336: - Flexibility: The Lower Half implements specific operation interfaces for different hardware, facilitating adaptation to multiple platforms. 337: - Modularity: The separation of responsibilities between the upper and lower halves reduces coupling, making code maintenance and extension easier. 338: 339: Through this hierarchical design, openvela's driver development can meet hardware adaptation requirements while maintaining code universality and maintainability. 340: 341: #### I3C Driver Framework 342: 343: I3C is more complex than I2C. In addition to hardware improvements, it is reflected in the following aspects at the functional level: 344: 345: - Addressing and access based on dynamic addresses. 346: - Support for CCC (Common Command Codes) commands, enabling extension of business requirements. 347: - Support for data transmission and reception based on I3C devices. 348: - Compatibility with data transmission and reception for I2C devices. 349: 350: 351: 352: 353: 354: #### RTC Driver Framework 355: 356: - **Driver Model** 357: 358: - **Lower Half:** This layer is hardware-specific and interfaces directly with the RTC chip. The primary task for a driver developer is to implement the `struct rtc_ops_s`. This structure defines a standard set of operations (e.g., `initialize`, `read_time`, `set_time`) that abstract the underlying hardware behavior. 359: - **Upper Half:** This is the generic, hardware-agnostic logic layer provided by openvela. It is responsible for creating a standard character device node (e.g., `/dev/rtc0`) and translating user-space VFS (Virtual File System) file operations, such as `ioctl`, into calls to the lower-half `rtc_ops_s` interface. 360: 361: - **Access Paths** 362: 363: - **User-space Access (Application Level)** 364: 365: - Applications interact with the RTC through its device node, `/dev/rtc0`. 366: - All communication is handled via standard C library file operations, for example, by using `ioctl()` to send commands like `RTC_RD_TIME` or `RTC_SET_TIME`. 367: 368: - **Kernel-space Access (Kernel Level)** 369: 370: - The kernel or other board-specific code can interact directly with the RTC using the `up_rtc_...` API family. 371: - These APIs provide a direct path that bypasses the VFS layer, allowing for direct calls to the lower-half driver operations. This approach is typically used during system initialization or in performance-critical scenarios. It works by acquiring a handle to the lower-half driver to operate on the hardware directly. 372: 373: 374: 375: 376: 377: #### IR Driver Framework 378: 379: The IR driver framework adopts an industry-standard **layered architecture**, dividing the driver into an **Upper Half** and a **Lower Half**. This design decouples the hardware-agnostic generic logic from the hardware-specific implementation, greatly enhancing code portability and reusability. 380: 381: 1. Upper Half: The Generic Logic Layer 382: 383: The Upper Half is responsible for implementing the hardware-independent core driver logic, providing a standard interface for the kernel and user-space applications. Its primary responsibilities include: 384: 385: - Device Registration: Registers the driver as a standard character device (e.g., `/dev/lirc0`), making it accessible from user-space. 386: - File Operations Interface: Implements the standard `file_operations` set (e.g., `open`, `read`, `ioctl`) to respond to system calls from user-space. 387: - Data Buffering: Features a built-in Ring Buffer to temporarily store infrared data reported by the Lower Half. This effectively prevents data loss and decouples the real-time intensive hardware interrupts from user-space read operations. 388: - Polling Mechanism: Provides a `poll` mechanism, allowing applications to wait for new data efficiently and avoid inefficient CPU polling. 389: 390: 2. Lower Half: The Hardware Abstraction Layer 391: 392: The Lower Half communicates directly with the physical infrared controller hardware, acting as the bridge between the generic logic of the Upper Half and the physical hardware. Its core tasks are: 393: 394: - Hardware Interaction and Data Reporting: Responsible for receiving and decoding infrared signals from the hardware, then pushing the data to the Upper Half's ring buffer through a designated interface (e.g., `lirc_xxx_event`). 395: - Hardware Transmission: Provides a transmission interface (e.g., `tx_xxx`) that can be called by the Upper Half to send infrared signals via the hardware. 396: - Hardware Control Interface: Implements a set of hardware-specific `operations`. These operations are exposed to user-space through `ioctl` commands, allowing applications to perform low-level configuration and control of the hardware. 397: 398: 399: 400: ### 4. 1: # FAQ and Best Practices
2: 
3: \[ English | [简体中文](../../../zh-cn/device_dev_guide/driver/driver-troubleshooting-guide.md) \]
4: 
5: This document provides a troubleshooting guide and best practices for `openvela` driver developers. Driver development requires not only hardware expertise but also a deep understanding of the operating system (OS) mechanisms. Many developers encounter issues with initialization timing, API calls, memory management, and concurrency control when adapting new drivers.
6: 
7: This guide systematically explains these typical problems and provides proven solutions to improve development efficiency and code quality.
8: 
9: ## I. Driver Initialization: Ensuring Correct Timing and Dependencies
10: 
11: Proper initialization is the cornerstone of stable driver operation. The driver's initialization logic must strictly adhere to the system's boot sequence and resource dependencies; otherwise, it can lead to a series of unpredictable issues.
12: 
13: ### 1. Delay Initialization for Operations Dependent on the File System
14: 
15: - **Symptom:** Calling file operation interfaces (e.g., `open()`, `read()`) fails during the driver initialization phase.
16: 
17: - **Cause:** File operations depend on the successful mounting of the file system. In the `openvela` boot process, core drivers and system services have a specific initialization order. If a driver initializes too early, the file system will not be ready, and related calls will fail.
18: 
19: - **Solution:** You should move the driver initialization logic that depends on the file system into the `board_app_finalinitialize()` function, which is executed late in the system startup process. This function is called after all core system services (including the file system) have been initialized, ensuring that all dependencies are available.
20: 
21: - **Related Documentation:** [Boot Process](../kernel/boot_process.md)
22: 
23: ### 2. Wait for Communication Readiness for Operations Dependent on Remote Nodes
24: 
25: - **Symptom:** Communication with a remote processing core (e.g., another chip) fails within the driver.
26: 
27: - **Cause:** Cross-chip communication depends on the complete startup of the remote system and the initialization of messaging components (e.g., `rpmsg`). Attempting to communicate prematurely will result in failure.
28: 
29: - **Solution:** You must postpone the initialization or communication logic for such drivers. You can use synchronization mechanisms like semaphores or event flags to wait for a signal indicating that the remote system and the local `rpmsg` device are ready before executing the relevant operations.
30: 
31: ### 3. Execute Operations Dependent on the KVDB Service After It Starts
32: 
33: - **Symptom:** Accessing the Key-Value Database (KVDB) within a driver causes the system to hang or the service to be unavailable.
34: 
35: - **Cause:** As a system-level service, KVDB is typically started by a system initialization script (e.g., `rc.sysinit`). Any calls to it before its initialization is complete will fail or block.
36: 
37: - **Solution:** Place driver initialization logic or functional calls that depend on KVDB within the `board_app_finalinitialize()` function, or execute them only after confirming that the `kvdb` service is running.
38: 
39: ### 4. Avoid Time-Consuming Operations in Initialization Functions
40: 
41: - **Symptom:** The overall system boot time increases significantly.
42: 
43: - **Cause:** Driver initialization functions are executed synchronously in the system boot path. Any time-consuming operations (e.g., hardware polling waits, long `sleep` delays) will directly block subsequent processes, thereby extending the total boot time.
44: 
45: - **Solution:**
46: 
47:     1. **Remove unnecessary delays:** Review the code and remove all non-essential delay calls.
48:     2. **Use an asynchronous work queue:** If a time-consuming operation is unavoidable, you should submit it to a Work Queue for asynchronous execution. This allows the initialization function to return quickly without blocking system startup.
49: 
50: - **Related Documentation:** [Work Queue Development Guide](../kernel/IPC/work_queue.md)
51: 
52: ### 5. Avoid Using Large Local Variables in Initialization Functions
53: 
54: - **Symptom:** The system experiences a stack overflow during the `APP_bringup` phase, leading to boot failure.
55: 
56: - **Cause:** The stack space for the `APP_bringup` task during system startup is limited. Defining large local variables (e.g., arrays of hundreds or thousands of bytes) in a driver initialization function can quickly exhaust this task's stack space.
57: 
58: - **Solution:** You should use dynamic memory allocation (i.e., heap memory) instead of large local variables by calling `kmm_malloc()` or a related interface.
59: 
60: ## II. API Usage: Selecting the Right Functions and Modes
61: 
62: openvela provides a rich set of APIs, but when using them in kernel mode (driver context), it is crucial to select interfaces appropriate for the current context.
63: 
64: ### 1. Use the file_* Family of Interfaces for File Operations in Kernel Mode
65: 
66: - **Symptom:** Using a file descriptor (fd) to operate on files within a driver leads to access exceptions or data corruption.
67: 
68: - **Cause:** File descriptors are bound to the context of a specific process (or task). A driver's execution context can change at any time (e.g., in an interrupt or a call from a different task). Using standard I/O interfaces based on `fd` (e.g., `read()`, `write()`) in this situation will cause errors due to context mismatch.
69: 
70: - **Solution:** In kernel code such as drivers, you must use kernel-specific file operation interfaces like `file_open()`, `file_read()`, and `file_write()`. These interfaces do not depend on a process context, ensuring operational correctness.
71: 
72: ### 2. Use Non-Interruptible Wait APIs to Avoid Signal Interference
73: 
74: - **Symptom:** Calling `nxsem_wait()` or another interruptible wait function returns prematurely before the timeout is reached, causing subsequent logic to fail.
75: 
76: - **Cause:** APIs like `nxsem_wait()` are **interruptible**. They can be interrupted by system signals and will return early (with a return value of `EINTR`). If your driver logic does not handle this case, it will lead to unexpected behavior.
77: 
78: - **Solution:** If your driver logic must not be interrupted by signals, you should use the corresponding **non-interruptible** version, such as `nxsem_wait_uninterruptible()`. This type of function ignores signals, waiting until the resource is available or a timeout occurs.
79: 
80: ### 3. Use up_udelay for Microsecond-Level Busy-Waiting
81: 
82: - **Symptom:** Using `usleep()` in initialization or other timing-critical scenarios causes hardware state anomalies or initialization failure.
83: 
84: - **Cause:** The `usleep()` function triggers the OS scheduler, causing the current task to yield the CPU. This context switch introduces an unpredictable delay, far exceeding microseconds, which disrupts the precise timing relationship between the driver and the hardware.
85: 
86: - **Solution:** For precise, non-schedulable, microsecond-level delays (busy-waiting), you must use `up_udelay()`. This function consumes time via a busy-wait loop without causing a task switch.
87: 
88: ## III. Memory Management: Optimizing Allocation and Alignment
89: 
90: In resource-constrained embedded systems, using memory efficiently and prudently is critical.
91: 
92: ### 1. Avoid Frequent Memory Allocation and Deallocation in I/O Paths
93: 
94: - **Symptom:** After the system has been running for a long time, it fails to allocate a moderately large contiguous block of memory, and system performance degrades, even though plenty of total memory remains.
95: 
96: - **Cause:** Repeatedly allocating and freeing small chunks of memory in frequently called paths, such as I/O handlers, causes the system heap to be continuously fragmented and coalesced. This eventually leads to a large number of small, non-contiguous memory blocks, known as **external fragmentation**, which reduces effective memory utilization.
97: 
98: - **Solution:** For such scenarios, you should adopt a **persistent** memory strategy. Allocate the required buffer once during driver initialization and reuse it throughout the driver's lifecycle.
99: 
100: ### 2. Use memalign to Meet Hardware Alignment Requirements
101: 
102: - **Symptom:** DMA (Direct Memory Access) transfers fail or data is corrupted; performance is poor when accessing certain memory regions.
103: 
104: - **Cause:** Many hardware peripherals (especially DMA controllers) require the memory buffers they operate on to have a specific address alignment (e.g., 32-byte or 64-byte aligned). Memory allocated by standard interfaces like `kmm_malloc()` is not guaranteed to meet such alignment requirements.
105: 
106: - **Solution:** When allocating memory for hardware that requires specific alignment, you must use the `kmm_memalign()` interface. This function allows you to specify the alignment boundary to obtain a memory address that meets the hardware's requirements.
107: 
108: ## IV. Concurrency Control: Proper Use of Critical Sections and Interrupts
109: 
110: Concurrency control in multi-tasking and interrupt-driven environments is one of the core challenges of driver development.
111: 
112: ### 1. Keep Critical Section Code Short and Efficient
113: 
114: - **Symptom:** The system becomes unresponsive, interrupts are lost, or resources within a critical section are not effectively protected.
115: 
116: - **Cause:** After entering a critical section (via `enter_critical_section()` or by disabling interrupts), the current CPU core will no longer respond to other interrupts. If the code inside the critical section takes too long to execute, it can severely impact the system scheduler and other critical services that rely on interrupts. Furthermore, performing any operation that could cause blocking or scheduling (e.g., `sleep`, acquiring a semaphore) within a critical section will cause the current task to yield the CPU while interrupts remain disabled, potentially leading to a deadlock or breaking the protection logic.
117: 
118: - **Solution:**
119: 
120:     - **Minimize the scope of the critical section:** Only place the absolute minimum, essential code that requires protection inside the critical section.
121:     - **Never perform any operation that might block or cause a context switch inside a critical section.**
122: 
123: ### 2. Register a Valid Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) Before Enabling an Interrupt
124: 
125: - **Symptom:** The system freezes immediately after a hardware interrupt is enabled.
126: 
127: - **Cause:** When an interrupt occurs, the processor jumps to the address specified in the interrupt vector table. If you enable an interrupt via `irq_enable()` but have not registered a valid Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) for that interrupt number using `irq_attach()`, the processor will jump to an uninitialized address or a default infinite-loop handler. If the ISR fails to properly clear the hardware's interrupt flag, the interrupt will trigger repeatedly, creating an **interrupt storm** that completely locks up the system.
128: 
129: - **Solution:** Strictly follow the **"register first, then enable"** principle. Before calling `irq_enable()`, you must ensure that a valid ISR, which correctly clears the interrupt flag, has been successfully registered for that interrupt.
130: 
131: ## V. Variable Usage: Ensuring Driver Re-entrancy and Stack Safety
132: 
133: ### 1. Prohibit Global Variables to Support Multiple Instances
134: 
135: - **Symptom:** When multiple devices of the same type exist in the system, the driver behaves abnormally, and the devices interfere with each other.
136: 
137: - **Cause:** Using global variables to store device state causes all device instances to share the same data. This breaks the driver's independence and re-entrancy, leading to one device's operations unintentionally modifying another's state.
138: 
139: - **Solution:** You must encapsulate the state data for each device instance in a private structure. Allocate such a structure for each device during its initialization and access it via a context pointer (e.g., the `priv` member) in the driver.
140: 
141: ### 2. Use Heap Memory Instead of Large Local Variables
142: 
143: - **Symptom:** The application crashes due to a stack overflow when calling the driver from user space via interfaces like `ioctl`.
144: 
145: - **Cause:** Driver code can be called by threads from different contexts, and these threads may have different stack sizes (e.g., a user-space application's stack may be much smaller than a kernel task's stack). If large local variables are defined in a driver function, it can easily cause a stack overflow when called by a thread with a small stack.
146: 
147: - **Solution:** For large data structures, you should use heap memory (allocated via `kmm_malloc()`). It is best to associate this dynamically allocated memory with the driver's private data structure to manage its lifecycle uniformly and prevent memory leaks.
148: 
149: ## VI. Runtime Environment: Efficient Use of System Resources
150: 
151: ### 1. Prefer Using work_queue for Deferred or Background Tasks
152: 
153: - **Symptom:** Creating a dedicated kernel thread (`kthread`) for a simple timed or background operation results in unnecessary memory and scheduling overhead.
154: 
155: - **Cause:** Each kernel thread requires its own independent stack (typically several KB) and participates in system scheduling, making it a relatively **heavyweight** resource. For non-urgent, short, and deferrable tasks, creating a dedicated thread is wasteful.
156: 
157: - **Solution:** You should prioritize using the system's `work_queue` mechanism. A `work_queue` uses shared kernel worker threads to execute the tasks (`work`) submitted to it, thereby reusing thread resources and significantly saving memory.
158: 
159: - **Related Documentation:** [Work Queue Development Guide](../kernel/IPC/work_queue.md)
160: 
161: ### 2. Avoid Executing Long-Running Tasks in a work_queue
162: 
163: - **Symptom:** Other services in the system that depend on the `work_queue` (e.g., networking, USB) experience delays or become unresponsive.
164: 
165: - **Cause:** The `work_queue`'s worker threads are a shared system resource. All `work` items submitted to the same queue are executed sequentially. If your `work` item performs a long-running blocking operation, it will monopolize the worker thread, preventing other `work` items in the queue from being processed in a timely manner.
166: 
167: - **Solution:**
168: 
169:     - **Split the task:** Break a long task into multiple smaller, non-blocking sub-tasks.
170:     - **Reschedule the work:** At the end of one sub-task, use `work_queue()` or `work_schedule()` to reschedule the next sub-task, thereby yielding the CPU to other `work` items.
171: 
172: ## VII. Coding Style
173: 
174: To ensure code consistency, readability, and maintainability, all kernel and driver code in the `openvela` project (excluding third-party libraries) must adhere to a unified coding style. Developers should perform a self-check against the coding style checklist before submitting code.

5: ## I. Implementing Chip Interrupt Debugging  
6: 
7: When debugging the chip interrupt subsystem (`bringup`), vendors need to implement a series of architecture-related functions (`arch` functions) to accomplish the following tasks:  
8: 
9: - Initialize interrupts  
10: - Enable and disable interrupts  
11: - Set interrupt priority  
12: 
13: The following information provides specific requirements and implementation examples.  
14: 
15: ### 1. Required Interrupt-Related Functions  
16: 
17: The following are the interrupt-related functions that vendors need to implement, along with their descriptions.  
18: 
19: 1. **Initialize the interrupt system**, including disabling all interrupts, configuring the vector table position, setting default priorities, and enabling interrupts.  
20: 
21:     ```C  
22:     void up_irqinitialize(void)  
23:     {  
24:       // Disable all interrupts  
25:       // Set the NVIC vector location  
26:       // Set all interrupts (and exceptions) to the default priority  
27:       // Attach the SVCall and Hard Fault exception handlers  
28:       // Enable interrupts  
29:     }  
30:     ```  
31: 
32: 2. **Enable a specific interrupt**:  
33: 
34:     ```C  
35:     void up_enable_irq(int irq)  
36:     {  
37:       // Enable interrupt with irq  
38:     }  
39:     ```
40: 
41: 3. **Disable a specific interrupt**:  
42: 
43:     ```C  
44:     void up_disable_irq(int irq)  
45:     {  
46:       // Disable interrupt with irq  
47:     }  
48:     ```  
49: 
50: 4. **Set interrupt priority**: If the `CONFIG_ARCH_IRQPRIO` configuration is enabled, the following function must be implemented:  
51: 
52:     ```C  
53:     #ifdef CONFIG_ARCH_IRQPRIO  
54:     int up_prioritize_irq(int irq, int priority)  
55:     {  
56:       // Set IRQ priority  
57:     }  
58:     #endif  
59:     ```
60: 
61: 5. **Manage interrupt states**:  
62: 
63:     - Check if `flags` indicate that interrupts are currently disabled:  
64: 
65:         ```C  
66:         #define up_irq_is_disabled(flags)  
67:         ```  
68: 
69:     - Save the current interrupt state and disable interrupts:  
70: 
71:         ```C  
72:         irqstate_t up_irq_save(void)  
73:         {  
74:           // Save current interrupt state and disable interrupts  
75:         }  
76:         ```  
77: 
78:     - Restore the specified interrupt state:  
79: 
80:         ```C  
81:         void up_irq_restore(irqstate_t flags)  
82:         {  
83:           // Restore the interrupt state indicated by flags  
84:         }  
85:         ```  
86: 
87:     - Enable all interrupts:  
88: 
89:         ```C  
90:         irqstate_t up_irq_enable(void)  
91:         {  
92:           // Enable all interrupts  
93:         }  
94:         ```  
95: 
96:     - Get the current interrupt state:  
97: 
98:         ```C  
99:         irqstate_t irqstate(void)  
100:         {  
101:           // Get the current interrupt state  
102:         }  
103:         ```  
104: 
105: 6. **Handle inter-core interrupts**:  
106: 
107:     ```C  
108:     // Trigger an inter-core interrupt  
109:     void up_trigger_irq(int irq, cpu_set_t cpuset)  
110:     ```  
111: 
112: 7. **Set the secure attributes of interrupts**:  
113: 
114:     - Set the secure attributes for a specific interrupt:  
115: 
116:         ```C  
117:         void up_secure_irq(int irq, bool secure)  
118:         ```  
119: 
120:     - Modify the secure attributes for all interrupts:  
121: 
122:         ```C  
123:         void up_secure_irq_all(bool secure)  
124:         ```  
125: 
126: ### 2. Required Interrupt-Related Macros  
127: 
128: Alongside the above function implementations, vendors need to define a series of interrupt-related macros, which describe the configuration of the NVIC (Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller). These macros should be defined in the `chips/chip_name/include/irq.h` file. Refer to the [RTL8720C example](../../../../../nuttx/blob/trunk-5.5/arch/arm/src/rtl8720c/include/irq.h) for guidance.  
129: 
130: The required macros and their descriptions are as follows:  
131: 
132: 1. **First interrupt vector number**:  
133: 
134:     ```C  
135:     #define NVIC_IRQ_FIRST  (16)   /* Vector number of the first interrupt */  
136:     ```  
137: 
138: 2. **Number of interrupts**:  
139: 
140:     ```C  
141:     #define NR_IRQS (64)  
142:     ```
143: 
144: 3. **NVIC priority levels**:  
145: 
146:     - **Minimum priority**:  
147: 
148:         ```C  
149:         #define NVIC_SYSH_PRIORITY_MIN  0xff /* All bits set in minimum priority */  
150:         ```  
151: 
152:     - **Default priority**:  
153: 
154:         ```C  
155:         #define NVIC_SYSH_PRIORITY_DEFAULT  0x40 /* Midpoint is the default */  
156:         ```  
157: 
158:     - **Maximum priority**:  
159: 
160:         ```C  
161:         #define NVIC_SYSH_PRIORITY_MAX   0x00 /* Zero is maximum priority */  
162:         ```  
163: 
164:     - **Priority step size**:  
165: 
166:         ```C  
167:         #define NVIC_SYSH_PRIORITY_STEP 0x40 /* Three bits priority used, bits[7-6] as group */  
168:         ```  
169: 
170:     - **Sub-priority step size**:  
171: 
172:         ```C  
173:         #define NVIC_SYSH_PRIORITY_SUBSTEP  0x20 /* Three bits priority used, bit[5] as sub */  
174:         ```  
175: 
176: ---
177: 
178: ## II. Binding Interrupt Handlers  
179: 
180: During interrupt processing, handlers can be bound using the following three methods. Each method is suitable for different scenarios and has its own advantages and disadvantages.  
181: 
182: ### 1. Using `irq_attach`  
183: 
184: ```C
185: int irq_attach(int irq, xcpt_t isr, FAR void *arg)
186: ```
187: 
188: 1. **Mechanism**:  
189: 
190:     - When the interrupt is triggered, `isr` is called in the interrupt context.  
191:     - The advantage of this method is high efficiency since the interrupt handling is completed directly in the interrupt context.  
192:     - During the execution of `isr`, all interrupts are masked, making it less suitable for systems with high real-time requirements.  
193:     - Blocking APIs (e.g., `sleep`, `wait`) cannot be called within `isr`.  
194: 
195: 2. **Unbinding**:  
196: 
197:     ```C  
198:     irq_detach(irq)  
199:     ```  
200: 
201: 3. **Advantages and Disadvantages**:  
202: 
203:     - **Advantages**: High processing efficiency.  
204:     - **Disadvantages**: Interrupts are masked during processing, which affects the real-time performance of the system.  
205: 
206: ### 2. Using `irq_attach_thread`  
207: 
208: ```C
209: int irq_attach_thread(int irq, xcpt_t isr, xcpt_t isrthread, FAR void *arg, int priority, int stack_size)
210: ```
211: 
212: 1. **Mechanism**:  
213: 
214:     - Users need to provide one or two handler functions:  
215:         - `isr` is called in the interrupt context, typically to mask the current interrupt and quickly wake up `isrthread`.  
216:         - `isrthread` is called in the thread context to handle the remaining interrupt tasks.  
217:     - If `isr` is `NULL`, `isrthread` is invoked directly.  
218: 
219: 2. **Advantages**:  
220: 
221:     - The execution time of `isr` is minimized, improving the system's real-time performance.  
222:     - `isrthread` runs as a thread, supports priority scheduling, and can be preempted by other higher-priority tasks.  
223: 
224: 3. **Disadvantages**:  
225: 
226:     - Consumes more memory (independent thread stacks and interrupt thread structures).  
227:     - Introduces an additional context switch, reducing execution efficiency.  
228:     - There may be a delay (approximately 5 microseconds) in completing interrupt handling.  
229: 
230: 4. **Unbinding**:  
231: 
232:     ```C  
233:     irq_detach_thread(irq)  
234:     ```  
235: 
236: ### 3. Using `irq_attach_wqueue`  
237: 
238: ```C
239: int irq_attach_wqueue(int irq, xcpt_t isr, xcpt_t isrwork, FAR void *arg, int priority)
240: ```
241: 
242: 1. **Mechanism**:  
243: 
244:     - Users need to provide one or two handler functions:  
245:         - `isr` is called in the interrupt context.  
246:         - `isrwork` is called in the work queue context.  
247:     - The key difference from `irq_attach_thread` is that `isrwork` is executed in the work queue instead of an independent thread.  
248: 
249: 2. **Advantages**:  
250: 
251:     - Interrupts with the same priority can share the same work queue, saving memory.  
252:     - High-priority work queues can preempt lower-priority queues.  
253:     - This method is more memory-efficient than `irq_attach_thread` when dealing with many interrupts.  
254: 
255: 3. **Disadvantages**:  
256: 
257:     - If there is only one interrupt, creating a work queue introduces additional overhead.  
258:     - In multi-core systems, there is limited flexibility in controlling thread attributes and the number of threads.  
259: 
260: 4. **Unbinding**:  
261: 
262:     ```C  
263:     irq_detach_wqueue(irq)  
264:     ```  
265: 
266: ### Summary Comparison  
267: 
268: | Binding Method    | Advantages                                                    | Disadvantages                                                                                   | Use Cases                                                        |
269: | :---------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------ | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------- |
270: | irq_attach        | High efficiency, direct handling in the interrupt context.    | Interrupts are masked during handling, unsuitable for systems with high real-time requirements. | Scenarios with simple processing and low real-time requirements. |
271: | irq_attach_thread | Improves real-time performance, supports priority scheduling. | Consumes more memory, introduces context switches, and has some delay in processing completion. | Scenarios with high real-time requirements.                      |
272: | irq_attach_wqueue | Saves memory, supports work queue reuse.                      | Low efficiency for single-interrupt scenarios, limited flexibility in multi-core systems.       | Scenarios with many interrupts and limited memory resources.     |
273: 
274: ## III. Implementation Example of Interrupt Thread/Work Queue  
275: 
276: Below is an example of binding interrupts and implementing interrupt threads or work queues.
277: 
278: ### 1. Binding Interrupts  
279: 
280: Use the `irq_attach_work` function to bind an interrupt handler:  
281: 
282: ```C
283: irq_attach_work(IRQ, isrhandle, isrwork, arg, 253)
284: ```
285: 
286: - `isrhandle`: The interrupt handler function, executed in the interrupt context.  
287: - `isrwork`: The interrupt thread or work queue handler function, executed in the thread context.  
288: - `arg`: The parameter passed to the handler functions.  
289: - `253`: The priority setting.  
290: 
291: ### 2. Example of Interrupt Handler  
292: 
293: In `isrhandle`, return `IRQ_WAKE_THREAD` to wake up the interrupt thread or work queue. If `OK` is returned, the interrupt thread will not be woken up. Example code is as follows:  
294: 
295: ```C  
296: static int isrhandle(int irq, void *regs, void *arg)  
297: {  
298:     up_disabled_irq(irq); // Mask the interrupt to ensure it does not trigger again after exit  
299:     return IRQ_WAKE_THREAD; // Wake up the interrupt thread or work queue  
300: }
301: ```
302: 
303: ### 3. Example of Interrupt Thread/Work Queue Handler  
304: 
305: `isrwork` is used to handle interrupt tasks and clear the interrupt state after completion. Example code is as follows:  
306: 
307: ```C  
308: static int isrwork(int irq, void *regs, void *arg)  
309: {  
310:   // Execute the interrupt handling logic  
311:   // Clear the pending bit of the interrupt  
312:   up_enabled_irq(irq); // Re-enable the interrupt  
313:   return OK;  
314: }
315: ```
316: 
317: ### 4. Special Case: One-shot Interrupt  
318: 
319: For certain one-shot interrupts, `isrhandle` can be set to `NULL`, and `isrwork` can be used directly to handle interrupt tasks.  
320: 
321: ## IV. Interrupt Structure Optimization  
322: 
323: When using interrupts, the system typically defines a global interrupt structure array: 
324: 
325: ```C
326: struct irq_info_s g_irqvector[NR_IRQS];
327: ```
328: 
329: Here, `NR_IRQS` represents the maximum number of interrupts supported by the system, which is typically greater than 200. However, in practice, only a few interrupts are used, and these interrupt numbers are sparsely distributed. This design results in the following issues:  
330: 
331: - **Memory Waste**: Even if only a small number of interrupts are used, memory must still be allocated for all possible interrupt numbers, requiring storage for `NR_IRQS` structures.  
332: - **Inefficient Resource Utilization**: The majority of interrupt numbers’ corresponding structures remain unused, leading to resource waste.  
333: 
334: ### 1. Optimization Strategy and Implementation Principle  
335: 
336: To address the issues above, the storage of interrupt structures can be optimized using the following dynamic mapping method.  
337: 
338: #### Mapping Relationship Array  
339: 
340: Define a mapping relationship array to dynamically establish the mapping between interrupt numbers and interrupt structures:  
341: 
342: ```C
343: irq_mapped_t g_irqmap[NR_IRQS]
344: ```
345: 
346: - This array only requires `NR_IRQS` bytes of additional memory.  
347: - The mapping relationship is dynamically established during interrupt usage.  
348: 
349: #### Simplified Interrupt Structure Array  
350: 
351: Define `g_irqvector` as:  
352: 
353: ```C
354: struct irq_info_s g_irqvector[CONFIG_ARCH_NUSER_INTERRUPTS];
355: ```
356: 
357: - `CONFIG_ARCH_NUSER_INTERRUPTS` represents the maximum number of interrupts that may be used in the system plus 1.  
358: - By limiting the size of the array, memory is allocated only for interrupts that are actually likely to be used.  
359: 
360: #### Interrupt Usage Statistics  
361: 
362: Use `g_irqmap_count` to keep track of the number of interrupts currently in use, facilitating monitoring and debugging.  
363: 
364: ### 2. Configuration Example  
365: 
366: Enable the optimization with the following macros:
367: 
368: ```Makefile
369: CONFIG_ARCH_MINIMAL_VECTORTABLE_DYNAMINC=y
370: CONFIG_ARCH_MINIMAL_VECTORTABLE=y
371: CONFIG_ARCH_NUSER_INTERRUPTS=24
372: ```
373: 
374: - `CONFIG_ARCH_MINIMAL_VECTORTABLE_DYNAMIC`: Enables the dynamic mapping functionality.  
375: - `CONFIG_ARCH_MINIMAL_VECTORTABLE`: Enables the minimal interrupt vector table.  
376: - `CONFIG_ARCH_NUSER_INTERRUPTS`: Sets the maximum number of interrupts that may be used.  
377: 
378: ### 3. Optimization Effects  
379: 
380: - **Memory Saving**: Allocates memory only for interrupts in use, avoiding waste for unused interrupt numbers.  
381: - **Flexibility Improvement**: Supports sparsely distributed interrupt numbers through dynamic mapping.  
382: - **Scalability**: Flexibly adjusts the interrupt limit via configuration macros.  
383: 
384: ## V. Related Repository
385:

The process begins at the kernel entry point, `nx_start`, and proceeds through several initialization stages within different task contexts before finally entering the `idle` loop. 10: 11: ### Core Initialization Sequence 12: 13: ```C 14: // --- In Idle Task context --- 15: nx_start() 16: | 17: +--> board_early_initialize() 18: | 19: +--> // Creates the AppBringup_task thread 20: // --- In AppBringup_task context --- 21: board_late_initialize() 22: | 23: +--> // Creates the nsh_task thread 24: // --- In nsh_task context --- 25: board_app_initialize() 26: | 27: +--> rc.sysinit // Script execution 28: | 29: +--> board_app_finalinitialize() 30: | 31: +--> rcS // Script execution 32: // --- System enters the idle loop --- 33: ``` 34: 35: The following table details the purpose, execution context, and required configuration for each key function and script in the sequence. 36: 37: | Sequence | Function/Script | Execution Context | Description | Required Kconfig | 38: | :------- | :---------------------------- | :---------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------ | 39: | 1 | **nx_start** | Idle Task | The openvela operating system entry point. | | 40: | 2 | **board_early_initialize** | Idle Task | Performs early board-level hardware initialization.
**Note**: This stage runs before core OS components are ready, so it **must not** call any function that could block or wait for an event (e.g., `sem_wait`). | `CONFIG_BOARD_EARLY_INITIALIZE` | 41: | 3 | **board_late_initialize** | AppBringup Task | Initializes the main board-level drivers.
**Note**: At this stage, core OS components are ready, allowing calls to functions that may involve event waiting. | `CONFIG_BOARD_LATE_INITIALIZE` | 42: | 4 | **board_app_initialize** | `nsh` Task | Called by the `nsh` task via `boardctl` (`BOARDIOC_INIT`) to initialize the application layer.
**Note**: The file system is not yet mounted, so file access is not possible. | | 43: | 5 | **rc.sysinit** | `nsh` Task | Mounts the file system and initializes core startup services. | `CONFIG_NSH_SYSINITSCRIPT` | 44: | 6 | **board_app_finalinitialize** | `nsh` Task | Performs final board-level initialization, called via `boardctl` (`BOARDIOC_FINALINIT`).
**Note**: Used for drivers that depend on file system access (e.g., TP, Charger, Audio PA). These drivers can now directly access files without needing to defer operations via the delayed work queue. | | 45: | 7 | **rcS** | `nsh` Task | Starts user-space core applications and services, such as `miwear` and `algo_service`. | `CONFIG_NSH_INITSCRIPT` | 46: 47: ## II. Startup Script Mechanism 48: 49: ### Location and Loading 50: 51: openvela uses the `rcS` and `rc.sysinit` startup scripts to configure the system during boot. These scripts are loaded and parsed by the `nsh task` via the `nshlib` library. Their locations are specified by the following Kconfig options: 52: 53: 1. `CONFIG_ETC_ROMFSMOUNTPT/CONFIG_NSH_SYSINITSCRIPT` 54: 2. `CONFIG_ETC_ROMFSMOUNTPT/CONFIG_NSH_INITSCRIPT` 55: 56: Typically, the startup scripts reside in the `/etc` directory. 1: # Contributing to Apache NuttX RTOS
2: 
3: Hi! Thank you for your interest in contributing to Apache NuttX RTOS :-)
4: 
5: ## Guidelines
6: 
7: To help us successfully review your contribution, it is very
8: important that you follow these guidelines.
9: 
10: If you need more information please read the [Full Contributing Documentation](https://nuttx.apache.org/docs/latest/contributing/index.html).
11: 
12: ### Coding Standard
13: 
14: * You should follow [NuttX C Coding Standard](https://nuttx.apache.org/docs/latest/contributing/coding_style.html).
15: 
16: * Your code will be automatically checked by GitHub Continuous Integration
17:   (CI) system. If you see the "check" step fails, it is possible that this
18:   happens due to style errors.
19: 
20: * Note that we require you to solve these issues and adapt all modified files
21:   even if you didn't introduce the problem yourself (this way,
22:   every contribution gets us closer to compliance).
23: 
24: 
25: ### Commits
26: 
27: * Each commit **must** contain a meaningful **commit message** that consist of:
28:   * **topic** (mandatory).
29:   * **description** (optional, separate with blank line from topic).
30: 
31: * **Prefix** commit topic with a functional context
32:   (i.e.  `sched: Fixed compiler warning.`).
33: 
34: * Provide only **signed commits** (`git commit -s`) with valid author
35:   and email fields.
36: 
37: * Valid commit message example:
38: 
39:     ```
40:     net/can: Add g_ prefix to can_dlc_to_len and len_to_can_dlc.
41: 
42:     Add g_ prefix to can_dlc_to_len and len_to_can_dlc to
43:     follow NuttX coding style conventions for global symbols,
44:     improving code readability and maintainability.
45:     * you can also use bullet points.
46:     * to note different thing briefly.
47: 
48:     Signed-off-by: AuthorName <Valid@EmailAddress>
49:     ```
50: 
51: * If you create a proper commit message as explained above, the first line
52:   will be automatically used as pull-request title and the rest is added as
53:   description. Use it as a starting point to describe your Pull-Request (PR).
54: 
55: 
56: ### Pull Requests
57: 
58: * Be sure to **fill in the pull-request report** with meaningful content.
59:   Be very descriptive, take your time. Good explanation, as for someone who
60:   can see the issue for the first time, will help understand the change and
61:   improve the assessment process. Please provide short descriptions even for
62:   a trivial change.
63: 
64:   * **Summary:** It is important to provide information on why change is
65:     necessary, what it exactly does and how, if new feature shows up,
66:     provide references (dependencies, similar problems and solutions), etc.
67: 
68:   * **Impact:** State how (where applicable) that change affects users, build
69:     process, hardware, documentation, security, compatibility, etc.
70: 
71:   * **Testing:** Please provide details on how did you verify the change,
72:     what Host was used for build (OS, CPU, compiler, ..), what Target was
73:     used for verification (arch, board:config, ..), etc.
74:     Providing build and runtime logs from before and after change is highly
75:     appreciated.
76: 
77: * Introduce only one functional change per pull-request.
78: 
79: * Provide finished and verified solutions.
80:   Clearly mark Work-In-Progress pull requests not yet ready for assessment.
81: 
82: 
83: ## References
84: 
85: ### Example Pull Request Report
86: 
87: #### Summary
88: 
89:   * Why change is necessary (fix, update, new feature)?
90:   * What functional part of the code is being changed?
91:   * How does the change exactly work (what will change and how)?
92:   * Related [NuttX Issue](https://github.com/apache/nuttx/issues) reference if applicable.
93:   * Related NuttX Apps [Issue](https://github.com/apache/nuttx-apps/issues) / [Pull Request](https://github.com/apache/nuttx-apps/pulls) reference if applicable.
94: 
95: #### Impact
96: 
97:   * Is new feature added? Is existing feature changed?
98:   * Impact on user (will user need to adapt to change)? NO / YES (please describe if yes).
99:   * Impact on build (will build process change)? NO / YES (please descibe if yes).
100:   * Impact on hardware (will arch(s) / board(s) / driver(s) change)? NO / YES (please describe if yes).
101:   * Impact on documentation (is update required / provided)? NO / YES (please describe if yes).
102:   * Impact on security (any sort of implications)? NO / YES (please describe if yes).
103:   * Impact on compatibility (backward/forward/interoperability)? NO / YES (please describe if yes).
104:   * Anything else to consider?
105: 
106: #### Testing
107: 
108:   I confirm that changes are verified on local setup and works as intended:
109:   * Build Host(s): OS (Linux,BSD,macOS,Windows,..), CPU(Intel,AMD,ARM), compiler(GCC,CLANG,version), etc.
110:   * Target(s): arch(sim,RISC-V,ARM,..), board:config, etc.
111: 
112:   Testing logs before change:
113: 
114:   ```
115:   runtime / build logs before change goes here
116:   ```
117: 
118:   Testing logs after change:
119: 
120:   ```
121:   runtime / build logs after change goes here
122:   ```
123: 
124:   How to repeat:
125:     * you can also provide steps on how to reproduce problem and verify the change.
126: 
127: #### PR verification
128: 
129:   * [ ] This PR introduces only one functional change.
130:   * [ ] I have updated all required description fields above.
131:   * [ ] My PR adheres to Contributing [Guidelines](https://github.com/apache/nuttx/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Documentation](https://nuttx.apache.org/docs/latest/contributing/index.html) (git commit title and message, coding standard, etc).
132:   * [ ] My PR is still work in progress (not ready for review).
133:   * [ ] My PR is ready for review and can be safely merged into a codebase.

1: # Code Style Checking Guide
2: 
3: \[ English | [简体中文](./../../zh-cn/contribute/code_style_check_guide.md) \]
4: 
5: ## Overview
6: 
7: This document describes how to use the **clang-format** tool for code style checking, including checking methods for scenarios with and without a default configuration file.
8: 
9: ## Checking Process
10: 
11: Different checking commands are executed depending on whether the `.clang-format` configuration file exists in the project.
12: 
13: > **Note**: The openvela project uses **clang-format 14** version for code style checking.
14: 
15: ### Scenario 1: Checking with Default Configuration File
16: 
17: When a default code style configuration file `.clang-format` exists in the project:
18: 
19: ```bash
20: clang-format -n <filepath> --Werror
21: ```
22: 
23: ### Parameter Description
24: 
25: - `-n`: Check only, do not modify files.
26: - `--Werror`: Treat formatting warnings as errors.
27: 
28: ### Scenario 2: Checking with WebKit Style
29: 
30: When a default code style configuration file does not exist in the project:
31: 
32: ```bash
33: clang-format --style=WebKit -n <filepath> --Werror
